title: Check if a given number exists in an array (linear search: loop through and compare each element).
shortTitle: Check if a given number exists in an array
keyPoints: Linear search scans the array from start to end, returning true at the first match and false only after checking every element.
The early return on the first match is the key efficiency feature: you stop as soon as you know the answer.
Best case is O(1) when the target is first, worst case is O(n) when absent or last, and space is O(1).
For money use BigDecimal compareTo returning zero to handle scale differences correctly.
Linear search works on unsorted data; for sorted data binary search achieves O(log n).
This is the foundation for contains checks in collections, dispute verification, and existence queries.

s1_definition.oneliner: Scan the array and return true at the first match; return false only after checking every element.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Linear search** – walk the array comparing each element with the target.
- **Early exit** – return `true` the moment a match is found, avoiding unnecessary work.
- **Worst case O(n)** – when the target is absent or at the very end, every element is checked.
- **O(1) space** – no extra data structures are needed.
- **Unsorted data** – works on any array regardless of order, unlike binary search which requires sorting.
s1_definition.analogy: Priya wants to confirm whether a specific cheque of Rs.9800 was ever cleared on her current account CUR3001 at National Bank of India. She reads cleared cheques one by one. The instant she sees Rs.9800 she says "yes, found it" and stops reading. If she reaches the end of the list without seeing it, she concludes it was never cleared.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Checking whether a value exists in an array is a linear search with an early exit. I loop through the elements comparing each with the target, and the moment I find a match I return true and stop. If the loop finishes without any match, I return false. The worst case is linear time when the target is absent, and the space is constant.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, I used linear search in the dispute resolution flow. When Priya disputed a charge, the system needed to confirm whether a specific cheque amount had ever cleared on her account. The dispute flow only needs a yes or no answer, not a count, so I stop at the first match rather than scanning the entire history.

For money I compare BigDecimal values with compareTo and check for zero, so an amount stored as nine thousand eight hundred matches one stored as nine thousand eight hundred point zero zero, because they are the same value even though their scale differs. Linear search is the correct choice here because the cheque history is unsorted. If the data were sorted I could use binary search for logarithmic time, but sorting first only pays off when I expect to search the same data many times.

Remember one sentence: scan until you find a match and return true immediately, or return false after checking every element.
